Pele Yoetz 109:11: And behold, the great fence is to think pure thoughts, that his mind be clear at that time and that he not be dulled with sleep, for then his heart is not with him and he thinks foreign thoughts and evil ruminations like one dreaming a dream - and of this it is said (Proverbs 19:2), "also, without knowledge, the soul is not good." And therefore I have said that on short nights, if he is concerned that he will not be awake at night, or if he awakens he will be dulled with sleep, in such a case the alert hasten - and it is better that he fulfill his mitzvah at the beginning of the night, and since his intention is pleasing to Heaven, his deeds too shall be pleasing, for they said (Nazir 23b), "a transgression for its own sake is great." And they wrote in the books that the essential repair of the offspring depends on the woman's own thought, in such a way that even if he is careful, if she is not careful, what has the righteous man accomplished? Therefore he should not fail to warn her and remind her from time to time, at every union, of this matter. And let husband and wife also be careful to examine themselves well and not need to relieve themselves at that time, for this causes children to wet their beds. And let them also be careful that their stomachs not be swollen and full of food, for this causes the birth of foolishness and folly and leads him to heaviness and laziness. These are some of the ways of those who straighten their paths, the path of the righteous - let the wise man hear and add learning, and may his offspring be pure, righteous, and abundantly good for fathers and for sons.
Pele Yoetz 109:12: And it is included in this, so that his offspring be a holy seed, that he be careful to guard against the nine traits that the Sages enumerated (Nedarim 20b), of which it is said (Ezekiel 20:38), "and I will purge out from among you the rebels and those who transgress against Me." And likewise let him be careful not to marry a woman who is not fitting, and let him investigate thoroughly through his relatives and inquire with seven inquiries until he knows what her character and nature are, for truly they said (Yevamot 63a): take a wife deliberately - for this is not a garment or a robe that, if it does not seem right in his eyes, he can strip it off and exchange it. Therefore let him watch very closely lest the days of evil come and a mortal blow, bitterer than death, strike the woman [i.e., a bad marriage]. And he should not marry a woman who is unfitting for the sake of money, for it withers and perishes like grass, while his own fire shall not be quenched. And since among the nine traits are "children of hatred," it is fitting for every man not to arrange a match for his sons and daughters except according to their own knowledge and good will - and in all this, a good sign is a matter: if the thing comes from the LORD and she is his true match, his own bone from his own bones, let him draw himself near, and she shall be with him in peace and uprightness.
Pele Yoetz 109:13: And included in what has been said is also this: that he not marry a widow, for she does not fully bind herself except to the one who first "made her a vessel." And it is likely that her mind still dwells on her first husband, and thus several minds are found in the marriage bed - all the more so if the first husband was pleasant to her and the second is harsher than him, for certainly she shall not forget the companion of her youth and shall despise the second in her heart. And moreover, they said in the Holy Zohar that whoever marries a widow enters into great danger, like one who casts himself to swim in the great sea. Therefore, whoever is a God-fearing man should not take a widow or a divorcee but only a virgin - unless he is advanced in years, or cannot find a virgin to marry, in which case he should not refrain from procreation but should take whomever his hand can find - these are wondrous matters known to those of perfect understanding, and the LORD shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 110:1: Zohar - The study of the Book of the Zohar is exceedingly exalted to purify and sanctify the soul, and even if one does not know what it is saying and errs in it many times, it is precious before the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written (Song of Songs 1:4[?], adapted), "and his banner over me is love" - our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2) "and his stumbling over me is love." What is this comparable to? A small child who knows nothing and speaks half of his words with a stammering tongue, and his father and mother laugh with delight and rejoice at his voice - so too the One who dwells in heaven shall laugh and rejoice when the Israelite man has affection for the Torah and wishes to study, but his own mind cannot grasp it, or he has no one to teach him, and he studies as much as he knows - certainly he gives peace of mind to his Former and shall come with his reward. Behold, therefore, there is no room for exemption for whoever does not know how to study - this excuse does not exempt him on the day of judgment, for he can study as much as he knows. And granted that in the study of the Mishnah and similar texts there is understanding required, that one must understand at least what the matter he is studying is about, but in the study of Psalms and the Holy Zohar, even if he understands nothing at all, it is precious, accepted, and pleasing before the LORD. And whoever knows how to read and understands the simple words of the Holy Zohar shall find in it good sense and words sweeter than honey and ethical lessons of the mind that draw a person's heart to his Father in Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 110:2: Behold, therefore, it is fitting for every person to take for himself the Book of the Holy Zohar and not fail to read the weekly portion each week - and this is a great fence for a person, so that his inclination not lead him to spend his time idly, which is a great evil, as is known. Let him do this and be saved: that he accept upon himself an order of study, such as eighteen chapters of Mishnah every day, and the Book of Psalms, and the Zohar portion, and the like - and when he has no leisure, he shall be a borrower and repay from day to day and from month to month, in such a manner that when he is free he shall immediately turn to pay his debt. But let him think about the matter from its beginning, that he not need to study so quickly that this study is worth nothing and his labor is for naught, God forbid. And they have already said (Tur, Orach Chaim, siman 1): better a little with intention than much without intention. And when he studies the secrets of the Holy Zohar, he shall understand in his heart that there are hidden secrets and secrets of secrets in every matter, but his own flesh shall grieve over him for having no knowledge whatsoever.
Pele Yoetz 110:3: And we have heard a warning for whoever studies the Book of the Holy Zohar, that he greatly guard his own soul when he studies of "Abba," "Imma," "Bera," "Bratta," "Ze'ir Anpin," "Arich Anpin," "Matronita," and likewise the forms of limbs, "Reisha," "Einin," "Udnin," and the like - that he not picture any form above, God forbid and far be it, for of this it is said (Deuteronomy 27:15), "cursed is the man who makes a graven or molten image and sets it up in secret" - in the secret place of the world. Rather, he shall believe with complete faith that these matters have no application above whatsoever - all is only supernal lights and hidden secrets that no hand of ours can reach. And all these words mentioned in the Holy Zohar are all figurative expressions and a mere manner of parable, which the enlightened shall understand somewhat and we shall not know, and we have no permission to conceive or picture them in any way - we shall only recite them with our lips and precede our prayer, that the pleasantness of the LORD be upon us, and that our lips' speech be accepted and precious and pleasing, to give peace of mind to our Former and His judgment.
Pele Yoetz 111:1: Provisions - Well known is the story brought in the Talmud (Ketubot 67b), that Mar Ukva, at the time of his death, saw the reckoning of his charitable deeds that he had performed, which amounted to seven thousand gold denarii. And he said: the journey is long and the provisions are scant. And he divided half of his possessions for charity - and although they said (ibid.) that whoever is extravagant should not give away more than a fifth, this applies during his lifetime, but at the time of death it is permitted. And a person shall see with his own eyes: when he goes on a journey, according to the road he travels and the number of days he shall be on the road, so must he prepare provisions for his journey many days in advance. Go out and reckon: according to how his own mind understands his stay in the world - length of years without number for him, he shall live for a man's thousand years - and even if he were to send ahead of him his own righteousness of a thousand thousand and myriad myriads of gold denarii, it would not suffice him.
Pele Yoetz 111:2: And if you say, since a person cannot fulfill his obligation to send to the World to Come enough for his own need, and "what shall we eat, you say?" - one must perforce say that the Holy One, blessed be He, performs kindness and a free gift - if so, even if we send nothing at all, we shall eat at the King's table. This is certainly vanity, for when a person does whatever is in his power to do, he is then sustained bountifully all the days of eternity in the World to Come, for the servant might say: I loved my master and would have wished to serve him if he had let me, and "better for me one hour of Torah and good deeds than all the life of the World to Come" (Avot 4:17) - and since the Holy One, blessed be He, removed him from the world, or did not grant him wealth to give more extensively, it is only right that he receive his full reward for all the days of eternity. Not so the wicked, who do not do what is in their power to do - they are given for the World to Come only according to the measure of what they did, and when the principal is depleted they must come back in transmigration to this world to earn more, so as to have enough for their own sustenance - and charity is not given for the World to Come, for if it were possible through charity, a person would not need to be born and be in this world, as is known from what the commentators wrote (see Yerushalmi Orlah 1:3), that the reason for the formation of the offspring is so that he benefit from his own labor, because whoever eats what he has not drawn up himself is hesitant to look him [the giver] in the face. And furthermore, the LORD shall say: why should I give you charity? Were you not able to earn and prepare provisions for your journey, and you did not wish to? What is this comparable to? Whoever throws away his own money to waste and then goes and asks for charity - certainly people shall be angry at him and shall not have mercy on him, and let no one be gracious to him. And if a person should say that the leaven in the dough - that is, the evil inclination - hinders him from being able to earn and that it is not in his power to act, would that this excuse exempt a person on the day of judgment - but the whole world knows that whoever has this excuse is not exempted by it.
Pele Yoetz 111:3: And from what has been said, you shall hear that the fact that a person fulfills his obligation by giving a tenth applies specifically during his own lifetime, so that he not become poor and need others - but an obligation rests upon him to instruct with all firmness, in a beneficial manner, that after his death they set aside for him from his own possessions a portion at the outset, according to the blessing the LORD grants him, to perform mitzvot and good deeds with it, and let him calculate how much is enough for his sons to be supported in an honorable manner, and let him take the rest for himself. And Rabbi Yehuda Ayash, of blessed memory, already wrote in his book "Brit Olam" (Sefer Chasidim, siman 344), in these words in brief: let a person take to heart that all his own salvation and all his desire is to leave his sons great wealth, and even if he has no sons, he is concerned for some relative, to leave him gold amounting to thousands upon thousands - and how does he not have concern for himself for the rest of eternity, empty-handed, in the World to Come, and has no knowledge or understanding to revive the heart of the downtrodden with what the LORD has graced him, which would be good for him as atonement for transgression and to draw near salvation and to prepare garments and delicacies for his holy soul? And although he is concerned for his son or his brother's son, in any case he takes precedence to take a portion at the outset for the repair of his own holy soul, and let him consider himself at least like one of his own sons, taking his own share along with him, to give to the poor, to Torah scholars, and it shall be stored up above - for what benefit shall come to his own soul from leaving his sons great wealth, while he himself goes empty-handed and is truly poor, and after his death shall go about grieved, and shall himself see the folly and ruin of his own deeds, and his pain shall be stirred and his own soul shall mourn over him - this establishes his own words. And I have been jealous of the reveling Ishmaelites, who at the time of their death leave a portion of their possessions for public needs or for their house of prayer - and why should we be lacking? Behold, therefore, whoever desires eternal life and not to need to come into the danger and evil of transmigration - let him do whatever is in his power to do, with his own body and his own money, and prepare provisions for his journey - then he shall go to his end and rest, and his soul shall delight in fatness, in light, and they shall give him an inheritance without bounds.
Pele Yoetz 112:1: Gluttony and Drunkenness - Gluttony and drunkenness are great evils, for their expense increases and consumes one's money and one's days and years in vanity and confusion - the day for work and the night for excessive eating and drinking, adding strength to the Other Side. And since he eats and drinks much, his mind is not sound and settled upon him, and most of his deeds are corrupted, and he permits forbidden things - and also, since he eats and drinks much, when he lies down he does not rise again until the time of communal prayer has passed, and many similar evils. And Rabbi Yehuda Ayash, of blessed memory, wrote in the book "Tziporen Shamir" (siman 5), in these words: they said in the teaching of the school of Elijah (Zuta, ch. 3): people do not gather toward death, and no creature descends into distress, except through eating, drinking, and the joy of the vanities of this world - and who is the man who shall hear the words of Elijah the Prophet, remembered for good, and not have his heart torn into twelve pieces, and despise wine-feasts and optional banquets and imaginary joys? And whichever way you look at it: if he believes the words of Elijah, remembered for good, and nevertheless deals falsely with his own soul, he is a fool and a simpleton striving to cause evil to his own soul, pain of body and soul; and if he does not believe it in any way, this is a bad, sick trait, and he shall surely be greatly punished for this too. And if he says thus: "such is the way of most of the world, and as we have heard, so we have seen - many wealthy men drink and become drunk, 'good is smoke to the mouth, good is a cup to the mouth,' no month and no Sabbath [i.e., every day is the same]" - you too say to him: come and see what becomes of them, besides the punishment of the World to Come, which is not revealed to our eyes, but which is true without doubt, as known from our holy Rabbis, of blessed memory, whose words all live and endure.
Pele Yoetz 112:2: And when a person considers that everything he eats and drinks shall turn within him into excrement and dung, shall he not be ashamed and embarrassed to make his own flesh and body a house of filth and a latrine? These ones prepare the foods and those ones defile them. And our teacher Maimonides, of blessed memory, has already written that a gathering of people for intoxicating drink is a greater disgrace, by right reasoning, than a gathering of naked men - except that through habituation it has become as though permitted and people do not feel it; this establishes his words. And truly, whoever has understanding and sets his mind to comprehend shall greatly despise pursuing eating and drinking, which involve great effort and little substance, for all the pleasure lasts but a moment, as it takes to speak, until the palate that tastes the food has passed, and afterward all the pleasure is forgotten as though it never was, and all kinds of food are equal in satisfying the soul, and all of man's labor is for his mouth and his palate alone - among all pleasures there is none so slight as this, and it is not worth the damage of loss and pain in this world and the World to Come, for body and soul. Behold, therefore, whoever has even a little understanding shall not be among winebibbers or gluttonous eaters of meat, and shall not walk on his belly, but shall conduct himself in a proper order, and through this the LORD shall be gracious to him.
Pele Yoetz 113:1: Sowing - It is good for a man whom the LORD has graced with even a small plot of land to plant fruit trees on it for the sake of settling the world, as it is written (Isaiah 45:18), "He did not create it a waste, He formed it to be inhabited." Go out and learn from the wild rooster, of which they told in the Talmud (Gittin 68a) how much effort and trouble it took upon itself for the sake of settling the world. And there is another good intention as well, for in everything that sprouts and grows from the earth, the holy sparks that are in that place begin to ascend from the inanimate to the vegetative, and afterward they shall ascend from the vegetative to the speaking [human], as explained in the words of the Kabbalists. And it is also included in this that he fulfills the counsel of the Sages, who said (Yevamot 63a): sow, and do not buy - even though they are the same [in cost], these are blessed - as is explained in the words of the Prophets through Jeremiah (29:5-6, 28): "thus says the LORD: build houses and dwell in them, and plant gardens and eat their fruit. Take wives," and so on. And behold, garden seeds not everyone can sow, for they require labor year after year, but trees one sows once and the seed remains for him and for his descendants forever.
Pele Yoetz 113:2: And the main good intention in sowing is that the man who fears the LORD in His mitzvot greatly desires and seeks ways to become obligated in mitzvot, that a mitzvah come to his hand to give peace of mind to his Former and to repair the matters at their root in the upper place. And behold, through planting trees, he fulfills the mitzvah of "neta reva'i" [fourth-year produce] and is careful of the prohibition of mixed species and the like, and he can fulfill something resembling the mitzvah of first fruits, that he take the first fruit that grows and bring it as a gift to a Torah scholar - of which our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 105b) that it is considered as though he had offered first fruits. And happy is he whose eyes are turned to serve the LORD in every occupation, and all his deeds are for the sake of Heaven, and he shall recite the blessings of heaven. However, in planting trees one must be careful not to plant except in a place he knows for certain is not fit for building, so that it not come to darken his light in a manner that he would need to cut it down - for although by law it is permitted for such a need, in any case the matter is not auspicious, and danger is treated stringently. Let him refrain from building if he would need to cut down a tree, and whoever is wise regarding the matter shall find good.
Pele Yoetz 114:1: Contempt - One must be very careful regarding contempt for others' honor, not to show contempt for their honor either in speech or in deed, and great understanding is needed to comprehend what constitutes contempt. And no one is innocent except one who is careful and alert to think very much before doing anything to his fellow, or saying anything to his fellow, or about his fellow, that he picture to himself: if his fellow were to do to him or speak to him or about him in the manner of this deed or these words, would it seem to him like contempt and would he feel pain? Then he should not do it to his fellow either. And they said, of blessed memory (Shabbat 31a): what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow - this is a great principle in the Torah. And truly they said (Nega'im 2:5): a person sees all blemishes except his own blemishes. And the sage said: there is nothing easier in the world than to find and recognize one's fellow's faults, and nothing harder in the world than to recognize one's own faults.
Pele Yoetz 114:2: And the complete man who fears the LORD shall not turn after gain, or after his own honor, or after his own bodily pleasure, to show contempt for his fellow's honor for his own honor, his own pleasure, and his own benefit - such as, if they suspect him of something not good, he should not say, "I did not do it, so-and-so did it," for they said explicitly in the Talmud (Bava Batra 164b) that this is called evil speech. And likewise there are wicked, sinful men who, in order to increase jest and revelrous joy, or so that the rich might laugh and grant them a handout, show contempt for an innocent man's honor and increase speaking scornfully of him (which in our language is called "mazkaria" or "zifkiliniar," and in German, "geringschätzung ist verachtung") - and they are like madmen shooting firebrands, making sport with this man's own blood. Woe to them, alas for them, woe upon them, for they have repaid evil to their own souls - evil shall come upon them, as they said, of blessed memory (Avodah Zarah 18a), that scoffing begins in suffering and ends in destruction, may the Merciful One save us, as we have written in its place. And whoever does these things, his own flesh shall grieve over him for having angered his Creator, for he thinks he performs a mitzvah in gladdening people, but in the end, those who do and rejoice in these evil things shall descend mourning to the grave if they do not take it to heart to repent.
Pele Yoetz 114:3: And how much must Torah scholars be careful, in their engagement with Torah or in their writing, not to speak words of contempt about anything that seems to them beneath their honor, if his fellow were to say it to him - and even if his fellow steps out of line and speaks harshly, he shall do his own part and guard a muzzle upon his mouth from sinning with his tongue. And especially in the presence of laymen, extra caution is needed to conduct honor toward one another in speech, so that they not say, "harlots painting themselves" (Shabbat 34a), and so on, and there be a desecration of the Name. And the upright man shall not show contempt for the honor of any creature, and all the more so for his wife and his servants - not because they are subjugated to serve him is he given permission to show contempt for their honor. And what advantage does a person have over his fellow? Is not the small and the great there [in the World to Come]? And even the servant may be freer than his master before the Omnipresent. Therefore, even if they transgress his will, he shall rebuke them with pleasant speech and guide them gently, as he would wish were done to him if he were subjugated under others.
Pele Yoetz 114:4: And even for himself it is not fitting to practice contempt and do something not befitting his own honor, for the Torah has mercy on the honor of creatures and exempted an elder from the mitzvah of returning a lost item if it is not fitting for his honor. And all the more so a Torah scholar, and especially one who is a leader of the community, must conduct himself with great dignity and not show contempt for his own honor, for the sake of Heaven, so that his fear and awe rest upon people and his words be heeded. And indeed they said (Kiddushin 70a): once a person has been appointed a leader of the community, it is forbidden for him to perform [menial] work in the presence of three people. And every Torah scholar must minimize his sitting in the synagogues of laymen and not speak with them so much - and this is not a category of pride, God forbid, for they said in the Talmud (Yoma 9b) that whoever converses with Reish Lakish is given a business deal without witnesses [i.e., trusted implicitly], and God forbid to think of Reish Lakish that he was, heaven forbid, proud - rather, it is fitting to conduct oneself with such dignity according to what kind of person one is, and one should associate only with his own kind according to his own wisdom and his own standing. (And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 52b): to what is a Torah scholar comparable in the presence of a layman? To a golden flask - if he eats with him, it becomes a silver one; if he jests with him, it becomes an earthenware one, and once broken, it has no repair.) Only for teaching Torah and learning it shall he humble himself like hyssop and converse with everyone, small and great alike. And likewise for every matter of mitzvah he shall act with his own honor and dignity, and this is his own honor - as we find regarding the great men of Israel who would do things themselves for the honor of the Sabbath (Shabbat 119a), and King David, peace be upon him, would dance with all his might before the holy ark, and said (II Samuel 6:22), "and I shall be still more lightly esteemed than this, and shall be base in my own sight." And it is written (Psalms 119:99), "from all my teachers I have gained understanding." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:1): who is wise? He who learns from every person. This is the straight path, which is honor to the one who does it and honor to him from mankind.
Pele Yoetz 115:1: Zemirot - How much praise there is for saying the Zemirot [hymns of praise] every day, whose secret is exalted and whose head reaches to the heavens, to cut down the tyrants and destroy all the external husks. And whoever comes late to the synagogue in a manner that he must skip parts of the Zemirot loses much good - all the more so those who, out of arrogance of spirit, study other lessons, Psalms and Ma'amadot and the like [instead], or sit in the sessions of laymen in the synagogue courtyard increasing conversation and skipping parts of the Zemirot - woe to them for the affront to the Zemirot! They are like one who exchanges pearls for pennies or potsherds - so it is with this matter, for even studying [other texts instead] is not good, and "a matter in its proper time, how good." And likewise it is not a good custom in some places to pause in the middle of the Zemirot to wait for the groom, or the sandak, or the father of the child, and the like, setting aside the honor of the Omnipresent for the honor of flesh and blood. And if it is difficult in your eyes to change this custom, wait for me until I appease you with words: if you were standing before a king of flesh and blood, standing and serving him and recounting his praise, would you pause in the middle for the honor of some person? Certainly not, for great is the king's honor, and it is not fitting to leave off in the middle of his praise and service for the honor of any person. If this is so for the honor of a king of flesh and blood, all the more so for the honor of the Omnipresent - and all the more so since from the beginning of the Zemirot to the end of the prayer, everything is one firm bond building His chambers in heaven, and it is not fitting to pause in between. Therefore whoever nullifies this, may his light shine as the noonday.
Pele Yoetz 116:1: Old Age - Once most of a person's years have passed and he has reached the age of forty, it is fitting to remember his end, for man goes to his eternal home and each day he continually diminishes. And if he did not remember his Creator in the days of his youth, and walked wantonly in the way of his own heart, and was drawn after the pleasures and vanities of this world, and did not look at the work of the LORD - now is the time for him to have mercy upon his own soul and to have regard for the honor of his Maker and to turn from his evil way to walk in the ways of the good and the paths of the righteous. Let him take heed and say: woe is me, for the day has turned, for the shadows of evening stretch out (Jeremiah 6:4). Let me now return to my own Husband, my Former, the One who made my glory and raised up my own head, before the days of evil come, days in which I shall have no delight, when I shall be able to perform neither merit nor obligation nor repentance. And let him say: enough is enough - until now I have done the will of my own inclination; from now on I shall return to my Former - perhaps He shall be pleased, and I shall correct my flaws before the day of my death.
Pele Yoetz 116:2: And the evil of man on earth is this: that the way of a man is right in his own eyes, and the inclination of a man's heart shows him evil - a hatred to choose to eat and drink and sing and dance, and, as a man of might, to leap like a hart and a kid, to pasture in gardens and to increase various kinds of jest and revelrous joy, and to make nights like days in gladness and merriment with beloved companions, young men and also young women, and similar evils. And when he grows old, his inclination leads him to say that now his strength is not as before and it is not befitting his honor to sit with young men in a company of merrymakers - rather, his honor lies with the great, to come among men and sit with dignified elders like himself; and on long nights they sit as princes, conversing about the land and its produce, about cities and kingdoms, and whatever comes under the lash of their tongue, speaking from one thing to another and from one matter to another to while away the time in a multitude of words, sending up smoke and coffee, and coffee again - and it seems to them that this is a straight and good and proper way, and that this is their obligation and this is fitting for them, and they neither know nor understand that this is carrion and this is a forbidden morsel, and both of these shall be burned in the house of ashes if they do not take it to heart to repent, for "in a multitude of words, transgression is not lacking," and woe to people for the affront to the Torah (Avot 6:2, Shemot Rabbah 41:8), as we have written under the entry "Dibbur" and in other places. Rather, this is the straight path that a man should choose, and especially as he reaches old age, let him remember the day of death and say: behold, now I have grown old, I do not know the day of my death - I shall repent today lest I die tomorrow. And let him cling to the wise and to books that teach a person understanding, and let him open his eyes to all his affairs, and not waste precious time when he is free, for the day is short and the work is much. On what shall he turn first - to repair what he perverted in the days of his youth, or to complete his obligation, a matter in its proper time? Therefore, whatever is in his power to do, let him do - repairs and study and mitzvot and good deeds, going on increasing until he is separated from the vanities and pleasures of this world and conducts himself with piety - perhaps he shall be accepted and say: happy is my old age, which has atoned for my youth (Sukkah 53a).
Pele Yoetz 116:3: And an obligation rests upon us to show honor to the elderly, for we find regarding the Holy One, blessed be He, that He showed honor to the elderly (Vayikra Rabbah 11:8). And it is found in the Midrash (Bava Batra 10b): they asked Solomon son of David, "who is a son of the World to Come?" He said to them, "whoever shows honor toward his elders." And one of the 613 mitzvot is to rise before an elder. And likewise one must show honor to the elderly in the order of seating, and even one who is young in years but wise shall let one greater than him in years sit above him, and should not say, "I am the wise one and it is fitting for me to sit above" - for it is a disgrace for a Torah scholar to take honor for himself and sit in the place of the great, and one must be concerned lest people gossip about him that he did not do well, and there is an element of desecration of the Name. Therefore let him sit below, and if they press him and raise him higher, then let him go up. And Solomon already said (Proverbs 25:7): better that they say to you, "come up here."
Pele Yoetz 116:4: And likewise it is fitting to show honor to the elderly by taking counsel from them on every matter. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Megillah 31b): if the elders tell you to tear down and the young tell you to build, listen to the elders, for the tearing down of elders is building, and the building of the young is tearing down. And even if the counsel of the elders does not seem right in their eyes, the young should not shame the elders' faces, but rather answer them with pleasant speech and in a manner of proper honor. And the elder too shall guard his own honor, and not bring himself to disgrace, and not do deeds unbecoming to elders, and also not speak in a place where he knows his words are not heeded - and through this his honor shall remain in its place. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Tanchuma, Miketz, 10) that a person should seek mercy for the days of old age, that he be healthy and free of the blemishes of old age. And well known too is their saying, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 44b), that a person should always precede trouble with prayer. Therefore let him pray for this too while he is still young (and I have already arranged a prayer for this, with the help of Heaven). And in any case, if he has some of the blemishes of old age that burden the members of his household, they must bear them and guide him gently and with honor, and "according to the pain is the reward." And let them be concerned lest they too come to this trait, and as one has done, so shall be done to him - and in any case, the blessed Name shall repay each according to his deeds.
Pele Yoetz 117:1: Reminders - How good and how pleasant it is to write a reminder for everything, whether for mundane matters or for matters of Heaven, for since forgetting is common and death is frequent, it is good for a man to write down everything he has done and performed, and all his business dealings, and everything owed to him and everything he owes to others - even from day to day he should not be lazy about writing a reminder, and likewise for everything he must do or that requires a reminder, let him do so. And I have made it my custom, when I drink water before coffee - since it is a common thing to forget the blessing "Borei Nefashot" [after drinking] - immediately after drinking the water, I turn my ring around to the back of my finger or to another finger, and through this I remember. And so for everything I need to remember, this is my way. And in such and similar manner, let every man make a sign so that he remember and not forget to fulfill everything incumbent upon him, whether optional or mitzvah matters, and through this he shall remember what is forgotten and find rest and be satisfied with clarity.
Pele Yoetz 117:2: And it is also good and fine to write down, in brief, reminders of necessary laws that one is not expert in. And how much shame comes to those householders who, every single year, are unsure and ask whether one must say "Shehecheyanu" on the night of the second day of the festival observed in the Diaspora, and likewise do not know the relevant and necessary laws of the Amidah prayer if they erred in something, and many other doubts in matters that recur from time to time - it is good for a man that when he asks once and is told the answer, he write it down and know what to do, and not be ashamed and never stumble again. And I have already written above, under the entries "Preparation" and "Remembrance," matters that require remembrance - see there. (And if the LORD is my help, I have it in my heart to write down transgressions and bad traits that many have trampled upon, and their severity, and the manner of conduct required, in a firm summary, so that a person may read what is written down every day and be drawn by his own hand, with the help of Heaven - may the LORD complete this for me and help me for the honor of His Name.)
Pele Yoetz 117:3: And there are ten remembrances that we are commanded to remember every day, written in the book "Seder Tefillat Chodesh BeChodsho" - whoever desires mitzvot shall not fail to remember them with his mouth and shall not forget them in his heart. And the essential thing depends on striving to attain the benefit that follows from remembering them, which was the Creator's intention, blessed be His Name, in commanding us to remember - for if one remembers without paying attention to what he has done and performed, but rather sets his heart and strives to keep and fulfill them - such as, in remembering the Exodus from Egypt, he shall remember His abundant goodness and His love and His compassion, blessed be He, with us when we were a nation in the midst of a nation, and His very capability, that He shattered the arrangements and broke iron locks and brought us out with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm - what no hand of ours can reach to understand, the great wonders He performed with us, and therefore we are obligated to serve Him with the service of a servant.
Pele Yoetz 117:4: And likewise in remembering the Sabbath, he shall remember that He is the Master of all works, for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth (Exodus 20:11), and abundant love is made known to us that He bequeathed to us His day of rest - He did not do so for any other nation - and in this too, no hand of ours can reach to recount how great is the goodness of the Sabbath.
Pele Yoetz 117:5: And in remembering the manna, and remembering that it is He who gives strength, let him take to heart that He is the one who gives strength to act with valor and gives bread to all flesh according to their young children, and whoever increases in trade gains no more, and whoever decreases lacks nothing - and through this he shall not labor to grow rich, and shall not turn aside from justice and truth, and shall trust in the Name of the LORD, that He is the one who impoverishes and enriches.
Pele Yoetz 117:6: And in remembering the deed of Amalek, let him take to heart the distress of Heaven, that the Name is not complete and the Throne is not complete because of our many sins, and let him set his heart to repent and repair his deeds, so as not to be a cause of harm.
Pele Yoetz 117:7: And likewise in remembering Jerusalem, so shall he remember, and shall sigh in bitterness and pour out his speech, seeking forgiveness.
Pele Yoetz 117:8: And in remembering the standing at Mount Sinai, let him take to heart the greatness of His love, blessed be He, and His delight with us, like a father who delights in a son, and how great is the goodness for the house of Israel beyond all the good things in the world, that He chose us and gave us the holy Torah - happy are we.
Pele Yoetz 117:9: And in remembering what our fathers did to anger the Holy One, blessed be He, let him take to heart His love and compassion in a time of wrath and His great patience with us.
Pele Yoetz 117:10: And in remembering what Balak and Balaam counseled to do to our fathers, let him take to heart, in order to know the righteousness of the LORD and His affection for them. And it all leads to one place, to arouse love, for it is fitting to love the one who has bestowed good upon us, and when we walked in a wayward path He loved us freely, and He performed wonders of kindness without end or limit, to a degree no hand of ours can reach, one part in a thousand thousand thousand and a multitude of myriad myriads - how great is His goodness and His kindness with us! Behold, therefore, it is not fitting to be ungrateful and repay evil for good, God forbid, but rather we are obligated to fear and to love - and let him reason a fortiori from flesh and blood, that if someone did him some favor, according to the measure of the favor he would feel it an obligation upon his own soul to love him and repay him well, all the more so is there no fathoming his obligation toward the Creator, blessed be His Name.
Pele Yoetz 117:11: And in remembering the deed of Miriam the Prophetess, let him take to heart the severity, weight, and great gravity of the sin of evil speech, and reason a fortiori, a fortiori twice over, from the deed of Miriam, as explained in the Talmud (Sifrei, Teitzei 25:9; Beha'alotcha 12:1; Avot D'Rabbi Natan 9:2), "and if Miriam," and so on. Go out and learn the severity of the sin of evil speech, that for none of the transgressions in the Torah did the Holy One, blessed be He, make a remembrance as He did for the sin of evil speech, and nevertheless, because of our many sins, all of us have strayed like sheep, and all of it is in evil speech. And they have already said in the Talmud (Arachin 15b) that it is more severe than idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed - let a man tremble and be seized and guard a muzzle upon his mouth. And this is the entire fruit of remembrance: that he take it to heart to serve and observe it, and at the very least, at the time of remembrance, he shall be aroused and take to heart what the mitzvah of this remembrance is and what reason there is in it, and shall not perform it as a mitzvah learned by rote. This is a great principle and a matter equally applicable to all the mitzvot of the Torah, and I shall write more on this below under the entry "Mitzvot," with the help of Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 118:1: Letter Chet: Desire and Affection - Desire and affection are greatly needed for every obligatory matter, for Torah and for testimony and for every single trait, and this is a matter entrusted to the heart, requiring the help of Heaven, for we know that this is our obligation, to serve our Creator with desire, affection, and great joy - but what shall we do, since our hearts are not aroused to this, and our own smallness and limited grasp are the cause of our own hindrance, and also our sins withhold the good from us, for our eyes have grown dim from seeing what the mitzvah is, how great is its goodness and its beauty, and how good is our portion and how pleasant our lot when we merit to give peace of mind to our Former, the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, and how great is the good stored up even for a mitzvah as light as the lightest of the light. Go out and learn from the wicked Nebuchadnezzar, who merited great honor and kingship in his own hand for four steps he took for the honor of the blessed Name (Sanhedrin 96a) - all the more so, the reward given to the righteous in the future to come. And let him reason a fortiori: if he has desire and affection for eating and drinking, which is pleasant to his palate for almost a moment, and for earning money, and other such pleasures of this world and human delights, which are vanity of vanities with no substance in them - all the more so for eternal life and giving peace of mind to our Former, who chose us to stand before Him to serve Him and bless in His Name, than which there is no greater good - all the more so should we have desire, affection, and great joy. Such and similar things let the living take to heart, and persist in this thought in times of leisure, to arouse love and affection.
Pele Yoetz 118:2: And whoever wishes to merit this trait, this is his way, the straight path: that he engage extensively in Torah and mitzvot even against his own will, not for his own good - let him press himself and nullify his own will before the will of his Maker, in the manner they said (Pesachim 50b): a person should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, for from not for their own sake he comes to for their own sake. So too in this matter: it is the inherent virtue of the pure mitzvot of the LORD to purify and cleanse the soul, and day by day his eyes shall be opened until the engagement in Torah and the fulfillment of the mitzvot becomes sweeter and more pleasant to him than all the life of the World to Come. And if some impure incident befalls him that causes him to neglect Torah and mitzvot, it shall be bitterer than death to him, for such is the very truth: what do we have from life if not to serve our Creator and cleave to Him, to give peace of mind before His throne of glory - and being distant from Him, our death is far better than our life.
Pele Yoetz 118:3: And behold, persistence in reading books of ethics and habituation to engagement in Torah and good deeds is a great principle - for if a person has practiced even a good custom of piety and an order of holiness, and one day it is diminished, it seems in his own eyes as though on that day he was not a Jew, and "if he heard it in the old, let him hear it in the new" (Berachot 40a) - but if he goes easy on himself day after day, the desire and affection shall go on diminishing until it becomes very difficult for him to keep and to act. And furthermore, it becomes to him as though permitted to neglect the mitzvah and the Torah and to transgress every transgression. Therefore one must be strong and of great might, to overcome like a lion, to stand guard over Torah and over service, and if his inclination overpowers him and defeats him, let him return and strengthen himself and hold fast, righteous man, to his own way, the holy way. And when he comes to fulfill a mitzvah that comes to his hand, let him precede it and take to heart things that arouse the heart to do it with desire, affection, and great joy, as is proper to do - and it is even better if he also says aloud, in these words: such is my obligation and such is fitting for me - and let him make an external arousal in his own body and his movements, and great preparation, for external arousal arouses internal arousal. And it is known that whoever comes to defile himself, they open the way for him, and whoever comes to purify himself, they assist him (Shabbat 104b, Yoma 38b) - a person who defiles himself from below, they defile him from above; one who sanctifies himself from below, they sanctify him from above (Yoma 39a), and one mitzvah draws another mitzvah, and everything follows the abundance of deeds, and great is study that leads to action (Kiddushin 40b), until he dwells in the shadow of the Almighty. Correspondingly, in matters of this world, he should have and show no desire or affection, for all is vanity and vexation of spirit - rather, let him act as one compelled by a demon and as one who has entered to relieve his own needs, hastening from the beginning to the end.
Pele Yoetz 119:1: Flattery - The great evil of flattery is explained in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in the Talmud and Midrashim, and the pure man, our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, gathered it in his holy book "Sha'arei Kedushah" - let the God-fearing man study it thoroughly, bind it with a firm knot, and let it be a remembrance between his eyes. However, one must explain what flattery is, for there are things that are not flattery, and there are those lacking knowledge who think they are flattery - such as, one who honors a rich man is thought to be a flatterer, while one who opposes them and shows contempt for their honor prides himself in his own folly, saying that he does not know how to flatter. But there is nothing correct in his mouth, for it is fitting and proper to honor the wealthy - as we find (Eruvin 86a) that our holy Rabbi would honor the wealthy, and Rabbi Akiva too would honor the wealthy. And the reason is that since the King desires his honor and has bestowed upon him from on high an abundance of blessing, we too are obligated in his honor, and especially if we have received from him some favor or benefit, obviously we are obligated to accord him honor. Furthermore, whoever increases in possessions presumably increases in performing mitzvot and good deeds more than others, and redeems his sins with charity, and it is fitting to have some concern for his honor even if he acted improperly and stepped somewhat out of line - one should not show so much contempt for his honor, for we find in the Talmud that they said (Pesachim 53a): "were it not for Todos, we would decree a ban upon you" - and they explained there that he would place merchandise in the purses of Torah scholars [to support them]. But the matter of flattery involves two manners, the first difficult and the second more difficult still. The first manner is that he shows a face and excessive affection to his fellow while his mouth and his heart are not equal, but rather with his mouth he speaks peace while in his heart he lays his ambush; or even if he is not his enemy and does not seek his harm, whenever he shows great love and honor beyond the truth that is in his heart, he has stumbled into the sin of flattery - and such things our Sages, of blessed memory, permitted toward one's wife for the sake of domestic peace, and toward one's teacher so that he teach him Torah, and also one may flatter the wicked for the sake of the ways of peace (Pirkei D'Rabbi Eliezer 37; and see Menorat HaMaor, siman 45).
Pele Yoetz 119:2: However, the second manner is evil and bitter - namely, one who says to the evil, "you are good," and does not rebuke and does not protest against one who has the ability to protest, for besides being seized [for punishment] for the evil as though he himself had done it, he shall furthermore surely be punished for the great sin of flattery. And the pure man, who sees the LORD, shall not show favor to the poor nor honor the great, and shall not spare himself lest his honor or his benefit be diminished, but shall trust in the LORD that He shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence, and whoever increases the honor of Heaven, his own honor increases and he shall not lack spoil - and let him roar like a lion and raise his voice like a shofar to protest against whoever has the ability to protest. And more is written on this below under the entry "Tochachah" [rebuke], with the help of Heaven. And Scripture says (Proverbs 28:4): those who forsake the Torah praise the wicked, but those who keep the Torah contend with them. And it is written (Psalms 139:21): do I not hate those who hate You, O LORD? Behold, therefore, showing favor to the wicked is not good, and it is forbidden to look upon the face of a wicked man - whoever publicly and defiantly proclaims that he is a transgressor and a habitual sinner. And it is fitting for every God-fearing person, even if he cannot protest, to at least flee from him and not show him favor and not accord him honor and not dwell near him and not desire his benefit, but rather he shall be despised and disgraceful in his eyes, and he shall honor those who fear the LORD. And because of our sins, flattery has grown strong, and there is almost no one innocent of this sin - but the man who fears the LORD and believes that God shall bring everything into judgment, since the evil of flattery is great, shall not follow the multitude to do evil, but shall overcome like a lion and do the good and the upright in the eyes of God, even if it is not upright in the eyes of men lacking knowledge, and shall manage his affairs with judgment according to the Torah, and the LORD shall be his help.
Pele Yoetz 120:1: Novel Insight - Well known is the virtue of one who originates novel insights into the Torah, which is exceedingly precious in the heavens above, to the point that they said in the Holy Zohar (Introduction, page 4) that he builds new heavens, and of him Scripture says (Isaiah 51:16), "to plant the heavens and to lay the foundations of the earth, and to say to Zion, you are My people" - do not read "My people" (ami), but rather "with Me" (imi) (ibid., page 5), for he becomes a partner with the Holy One, blessed be He. And every person is obligated only according to his own measure, but he shall labor with all his strength to originate novel insights into the Torah - that is, to raise difficulties and resolve them in Scripture and Talmud, or to offer interpretations according to the four levels (plain meaning, allusion, homiletics, secret) on Scripture and Talmud - and this is a great repair for every sin and every transgression, and especially for the sin of blemishing the covenant, since the seed comes forth from the brain, and its repair is that he labor with his brain to originate novel Torah insights, and especially on the Sabbath it is very precious to originate novel Torah insights, as they extolled at length in the Holy Zohar (part 3, page 173), what benefit reaches him and what honor and greatness is accorded to the soul of his father and mother (this passage of the Holy Zohar has already been published in the pamphlet "Orot Eilim"). And for whoever cannot originate novel Torah insights from his own mind, there is already a remedy: that he study novel Torah insights that others have already made and written in books - whatever he studies and comes to know that he did not know before is considered as though he had originated it. And for this let every literate person strive greatly, at the very least to study something new on the Sabbath, and if he is not literate, let him strive to hear from teachers something new that he did not know. And also the study of the Book of the Holy Zohar, even without understanding, is considered as though he had originated novel insights - and both one who does much and one who does little are equal, provided he directs his heart to Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 120:2: And whatever he originates, let him write it down in a book and not treat it with contempt, and likewise let him write down whatever new thing he hears - for the commentators have written that now that the Temple does not stand and there are no sacrifices, whoever writes novel Torah insights atones for himself as though he had offered sacrifices, and they support this from Scripture (Psalms 40:7[adapted]), "burnt offering and sin offering You did not require; then I said, behold, I come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me." And they also wrote (Sefer Chasidim, siman 530) that a person is destined to give judgment for the fact that novel Torah insights were revealed to him and he did not write them down, for they were revealed to him only on condition that he write them down and that others benefit from them, and so that the benefit reach him that his own lips move in the grave. And would that a person write down everything he hears of novel Torah insights from his youth - he could produce good things sweeter than honey and more desirable than gold. And although there are things already written down, there is much that has not yet been given over to be written - and in any case it would have been very good to gather together everything one hears of sweet and sharp words, and he would do a kindness to those who do not have those books, that they learn the matter from his own book, and through him and because of him, the Most High shall be praised.
